title: What five extra years change on a ₹40 lakh home loan
summary: Compare a 15-year and a 20-year repayment schedule for the same home, using one worked example.
imageAlt: A miniature two-storey home with a brass key on the step
bodyHtml:
Suppose you borrow ₹40 lakh at an illustrative annual rate of 8%. Keep the rate fixed for this exercise and assume monthly repayments with no fees or prepayments. What happens if you give yourself five more years to repay?

Two schedules for the same home

Over 15 years, the monthly EMI is about ₹38,226. Across 180 payments, interest adds up to roughly ₹28.81 lakh. Over 20 years, the EMI falls to about ₹33,458, while interest across 240 payments rises to roughly ₹40.30 lakh.

The longer schedule frees up about ₹4,768 each month. If you follow both schedules to the end, those extra five years add about ₹11.49 lakh in interest.

Try the comparison with your own numbers

Enter your borrowing amount and quoted rate in the EMI calculator. Write down both the monthly payment and total interest, then change only the tenure. For a floating-rate offer, repeat the exercise at a higher rate to see how sensitive the estimate is.

title: How much room does a home EMI leave in your budget?
summary: Build a monthly budget for a new home, including the expenses that continue after you move.
imageAlt: Homes facing a landscaped residential courtyard
bodyHtml:
A couple comparing two flats has ₹90,000 in monthly take-home income. One flat fits their deposit budget, but can they comfortably cover the monthly EMI once they move?

Start with a normal month

In their example, groceries, utilities, commuting and other essentials total ₹35,000. An existing EMI takes ₹8,000, and they set aside ₹12,000 for savings and irregular expenses. That leaves ₹35,000 for housing.

Include the costs of living there

The first society quotes ₹4,000 a month for maintenance. After reserving that amount, the couple has ₹31,000 available for the home EMI. The second flat has a different maintenance bill and a longer commute, so they repeat the calculation for that address.

Check the months around possession

If your rent and loan payments overlap, draw up a separate budget for those months. Put the expected moving date, last rent payment and first instalment on one calendar. Keep this household estimate alongside the eligibility figure your lender gives you.

title: Turn a processing fee percentage into a rupee amount
summary: Use the same loan amount to compare a flat fee with a percentage fee, including any minimum or cap.
imageAlt: Calculator, paperwork and a model home on a sunlit desk
bodyHtml:
Two sample quotes for a ₹40 lakh loan list their processing fees differently. One says 0.35% with a ₹10,000 cap. The other quotes a flat ₹12,000. Assume both figures exclude tax for this example.

Apply the cap after doing the multiplication

Multiplying ₹40,00,000 by 0.0035 gives ₹14,000. The cap brings the first sample fee down to ₹10,000. The second stays at ₹12,000, a difference of ₹2,000 before tax. If a quote also includes a minimum, check the calculated fee against both limits.

Compare like with like

For each offer, write down the loan amount, the processing fee in rupees and any separately quoted tax, valuation or legal charges. Ask when each amount is due and which payments are refundable if the purchase falls through.

Keep upfront costs and total loan interest in separate rows. A ₹2,000 saving today tells you about the fee difference. To compare the repayment cost, run both interest rates through the EMI calculator using the same principal and tenure.
